items.title: [ScienceDaily] Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
items.content_html: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

items.title: 🔓 [Scientific American] Quantum physics can now prove where you really are
items.content_html: In a first-of-its-kind experiment, researchers used a single photon and some-second timing to verify a location—a potential new defense against digital imposters

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
items.content_html: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered a new genetic eye disease that can silently damage peripheral and night vision while leaving central sight largely unaffected for years. The condition may be detectable through an unusual difficulty adjusting to darkness, offering a potential early warning sign before irreversible retinal damage occurs.

items.title: 🔓 [WIRED] Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die
items.content_html: Biologically important chemical reactions persisted in the sterilized soil for six years—offering clues to how life on Earth may have gotten its start.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
items.content_html: Scientists have identified a gene that helps the brain’s immune cells contain harmful plaques linked to Alzheimer’s, potentially revealing a new way to fight the disease. When the gene malfunctioned in mice, toxic buildup accelerated and cognitive abilities declined, raising hopes that restoring its function could help protect the brain.

items.title: [apnews.com] European-Japanese BepiColombo enters Mercury orbit ahead of two-probe science mission
items.content_html: BepiColombo, a joint mission of the European Space Agency and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, entered orbit around Mercury on Nov. 21, completing an eight-year journey and becoming the second mission to orbit the planet. The two orbiters remain attached; they are scheduled to separate on Dec. 9–10 and take up different polar orbits, with science operations due to begin in April 2027. The mission will use the European Mercury Planetary Orbiter and Japan’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, called Mio, to study Mercury from separate vantage points. Their instruments are designed to examine the planet’s surface and interior, its magnetic field and the thin gas envelope around it, including how the magnetic field interacts with the solar wind. Controllers in Germany confirmed the spacecraft’s capture several hours after a series of braking thruster firings, with the spacecraft about 152 million kilometers away. A propulsion-system problem delayed BepiColombo’s arrival from December 2025. Its nominal science mission is planned to last one Earth year, with an extension through 2029.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
items.content_html: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

items.content_html: The strange “dark comet” 1998 KY26 is moving in a way scientists have yet to fully understand. A Japanese space probe was set to visit in 2031, but engine trouble will prevent that encounter, leaving the mystery unsolved

items.title: [thejournal.ie] Anthropic AI proof clears formal checks, but human review remains
items.content_html: An AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis by Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge has passed formal checks by two groups: the Lean Focused Research Organization, which advances the Lean proof system, and the Mathlib Initiative, which supports its mathematics library. The groups said on Nov. 21 they had “full confidence” in the proof Alpöge developed with Anthropic’s Claude model. The checks establish that the formalized code proves the Riemann hypothesis as defined in Mathlib, but do not provide mathematicians with a readable account of the argument. The proof consists of a Lean library of about 17 million lines, and Alpöge has said the argument is too large to present as a conventional paper at this stage. The certification does not constitute formal acceptance of the problem as solved. The Clay Mathematics Institute requires a solution to appear in a peer-reviewed journal and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can consider awarding its $1 million prize.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why
items.content_html: Microplastics may be doing something far more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies. Scientists have discovered that tiny plastic particles can interact with water to generate highly reactive molecules capable of damaging cells and tissues. This unexpected chemical activity could help explain growing evidence linking microplastic exposure to serious health problems, including heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
items.content_html: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
items.content_html: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.

items.title: [sciencedaily.com] Researchers test lunar-soil bricks and oxygen extraction methods
items.content_html: University of Arkansas researchers used simulated lunar soil to print small, interlocking bricks without binders, while a separate team found that plasma treatment can release oxygen and oxygen-containing gases from lunar-soil simulants. Both experiments aim to reduce the supplies future lunar missions would need to transport from Earth, but neither method is ready for practical use: the bricks need to be stronger, and oxygen yields must increase substantially. The brick study, published in *npj Advanced Manufacturing*, used laser powder bed fusion; the oxygen-extraction research, published in *Scientific Reports*, adapted plasma processing used in semiconductor manufacturing. Researchers still need to test the brick process in lunar vacuum and low gravity and determine whether oxygen extraction can be improved and scaled up economically.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
items.content_html: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

items.title: [scientificamerican.com] Astronomers witness dying giant star engulfing companion in real time
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers watched a dying giant star in the Andromeda galaxy engulf and merge with its smaller companion, recording the process as it unfolded for the first time. The companion spiraled through the giant’s outer envelope for about seven years before the system erupted in October 2025. The observation provides direct evidence of a short-lived phase called common-envelope evolution, previously studied mainly through models. The James Webb Space Telescope observed the remnant 47 days after the eruption, but dust from expelled material now obscures the remnant. Researchers plan to monitor the system as it cools and settles over the coming years or decades.

items.title: [science.org] Brain study finds speech-planning region may aid communication devices
items.content_html: A study published Nov. 19 in Science identifies a small region within Wernicke’s area that helps prepare words before people speak, challenging the view that the area mainly processes speech heard from others. The region, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, became active before speech, and disrupting it caused speech errors in stimulation and lesion tests. Researchers recorded brain activity in 28 people undergoing treatment for epilepsy or tumors. Stimulation tests involved 13 people, and an analysis of surgical cases also linked damage to the area with speech difficulties. In two people with paralysis, signals from the region helped researchers decode intended and heard speech, suggesting it could be explored as a target for communication devices for people with language disorders. Researchers presented the findings at the Society for Neuroscience meeting on Nov. 15.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] ‘No one asked for this’: AI is being pushed on people—and they’re sick of it
items.content_html:
The AI era is fully here—and while companies bill it as a solution to problems, consequences like mass layoffs, environmental effects, privacy concerns, and the slopification of culture have many people fed up with something they never wanted in the first place.

The technology faces growing resentment from workers, who are being urged to embrace AI tools even as businesses have rushed to reduce their workforces in favor of automation. 

Online, many posts about AI capture a growing frustration with how these tools—and their disruptions—are being forced on users.

“Nobody asked for Google to be worse—but AI made it happen,” one X user recently remarked. “No one asked for computer hardware costs to rise—but AI made it happen. No one asked for human customer service to be replaced—but AI made it happen.”

In another post, Sarah Hoyt, a science fiction, fantasy, and mystery author, said she doesn’t hate artificial intelligence, but is “begging all the crazy people out there to stop pushing AI where no one asked for it.”

The disenchantment plays out in the data: In 2019, 81% of Glassdoor reviews mentioning AI were positive, the company said, compared with 43% this year. Meanwhile, Pew Research found that 52% of Americans were more concerned than excited about AI, up from 37% in 2021. And in an Ipsos poll from June, 67% of respondents thought AI would worsen the worker experience.

“The closest analog is the replacement of physical labor throughout the long Industrial Revolution,” said Jiemin Tina Wei, an assistant professor of history at Florida International University. But in this case, it’s “brain work,” rather than manual labor, that’s being replaced. 

“And now, the industries that are getting allegedly wiped out are the ‘low-hanging fruit’ of white-collar work,” she said.

But gutted livelihoods aren’t the only reason many are anti-AI.

The productivity paradox

Louis Hyman, a historian at Johns Hopkins University who specializes in labor and the American economy, points to a “productivity paradox”: a contradiction that was also generally true of the rise of computers in the ’80s, in which similarly dizzying investments didn’t necessarily make people better at their jobs as promised.

He points to snags like the frequency of software updates. “Every time you learn how to do something, suddenly they break it, and you have to relearn it.” With the introduction of AI, it’s “as if all software is being updated, all at once, everywhere.” Another part of the equation, he said, is that it isn’t clear how some people are using AI tools.

Hyman said he uses AI to write software and automate “boring tasks”—for example, he wrote a script to rotate the thousands of photos he takes of historical documents during archive visits so they all face right-side-up. But, he said, “most people are not wanting to sit down and write Python code to automate their job. They just want to do their job.” 

Added to that is the deep fear of being replaced once the work is automated. “I’m a tenured professor—I literally can’t be fired,” he said. “If I automate some boring part of my job, that just means I have more time to do the more interesting parts of my job. And that’s not true for all people, right?” 

A new occupational hazard

Another reason many people push back on AI is the lack of adequate guardrails—especially when it could cause major issues at work.

In one case, an AI tool deleted a software company’s entire database. In another, AI was blamed for deleting a fully edited season of a Swedish reality show mere weeks before the scheduled premiere. In medical settings, AI scribes have put inaccurate information in patient records, raising the question of who would be held liable for resulting medical errors. 

Meanwhile, misreads by AI identification tools used by law enforcement have led to wrongful arrests and injuries, per the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) AI Risk Initiative. Other AI-generated errors have popped up in court documents, federal reports, news stories, and fast-food drive-throughs. 

“The main point I’ve pushed and will continue to push [regarding] AI is ‘no one asked for this,’” radio host Adam Xii said on X, in response to news that Anthropic hallucinated details in its defense during a music copyright lawsuit. “So when a product or service no one asked for suddenly becomes ubiquitous, one must ask: why? Because AI tools are meant to generate more wealth for the wealthy at the expense of creatives.”

At the least, AI’s convenience is being offset by a need to check its work that has created new opportunities for human error. The proliferation of “workslop” even led a tech company’s CEO to fully ban AI use, as Inc. reported this summer. 

“A lot of what I’ve seen is kind of annoyance at the proselytizers at work—or the people who are heavy adopters—creating a lot of extra work for the people around them,” because those people downstream then have to check the work, Wei said.

Wei added that content moderation and data annotation work “can be extremely mentally taxing.” Research has found that “good” challenging work will be both difficult and interesting to certain extents, she said. But checking output is both difficult—because you have to look for every small potential error—and boring.

“You’re not producing knowledge, but merely supervising the production of words, knowledge, content,” Wei said.

The unwanted technological advances continue

AI’s intrusive nature—accompanied, again, by the threat of replacement—is reflected in workers’ behavior, not just in fed-up tweetstorms. One report found that nearly a third of workers surveyed, and 44% among Gen Z, had tried to sabotage their companies’ AI strategies.

Section, an AI planning and upskilling company, recently reported that 69% of workers surveyed said their organization had encouraged the use of AI agents, but only 16% actually used them. And 38% said they use other AI features.

The frustration hasn’t seemed to deter tech companies.

“We heard you wanted Copilot Mode at work,” read an X post from Microsoft that promoted Edge’s Copilot Mode for Business.

“No, you heard wrong,” a computer technician replied. “Literally no one asked for all this AI. In fact, everyone wants to know how to remove it.” 

Questions of organizations

In some cases, it seems companies are starting to discover that automation has some shortcomings.

In the U.S., 32% of hiring managers who eliminated positions in favor of AI have had to reinstate the same or similar roles, according to research from consulting firm Robert Half. Similarly, Gartner predicts that by 2027, half of companies that attributed reductions in staff to AI will rehire people to perform similar work.

Wei said the mismatch between the hopes for AI and the reality of its adoption relates to a quote from Bill Haywood, a famous labor organizer, who said that “the manager’s brains are under the workman’s cap.”

In other words, Wei said, “It’s really ultimately the workers who possess the knowledge and the know-how to run day-to-day operations. Some people have argued that the history of labor is just managers trying to take back that knowledge in an attempt to replace workers in the production.

“And I guess some people experience AI that way—that it’s being [imposed] upon them so that they train, ultimately, their final, automated replacement.”

Hyman said that a better alternative to the “adapt or die” mentality would be for organizations to use the technology to empower their employees. They should “actually say, ‘okay, we’re gonna create organizational conditions that let you replace yourself, and then focus on the work that needs to be done’—because the amount of work to be done is not finite, right?”

“I get told on a nearly weekly basis that historians are going to be replaced,” Hyman said. “So, yeah, it depends on how valuable you think getting reliable information and history is.”

He added that a world “where the only source of history or journalism is from either Open AI or Anthropic” would feel like an “Orwellian nightmare.”

“That seems not a great road to go down,” he said.

items.title: [science.nasa.gov] Webb traces Andromeda star merger, challenging common-envelope models
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers say a smaller star spiraled into a red giant and merged with it in the Andromeda galaxy, marking the first closely tracked observation of this stage of binary-star evolution. The system, named AT 2025abao, brightened over several years before erupting in October 2025. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope observed it 47 days after the outburst peaked, helping researchers reconstruct the event. The team estimates that the giant had seven times the Sun’s mass and the companion about 0.7 times the Sun’s mass. Their interaction ended after about seven orbits, or seven years. The findings, published in Nature on Nov. 18, indicate that energy transport during the shared-envelope phase may be more complex than standard models describe. Researchers say continued observations are needed to determine the remnant’s state and confirm the merger.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
items.content_html: MIT researchers have discovered that the brain’s natural waste-removal system becomes significantly less effective during sleep as people age. The decline is linked to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and changes in blood flow, potentially offering new clues about why aging increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Surprisingly, some older adults retain the same powerful cleansing waves seen in younger people.
